overview: This one-page file consists of an airgram from the Office of the U.S. Political Adviser in Tokyo transmitting a December 3, 1949, Far East Command news release about the arrival in Japan of Stanford geologist Ben M. Page. Page was assigned to assist the occupation authorities’ Mining and Geology Division in improving mineral-exploration techniques, locating reserves needed for Japanese industrial self-sufficiency, and implementing earlier expert recommendations in cooperation with Japanese geological and mineral-exploration agencies.

subfiles.title: Airgram from USPOLAD Tokyo on Ben M. Page’s geological mission
subfiles.about: Transmits a Far East Command news release describing Stanford geologist Ben M. Page’s work to improve mineral exploration and identify industrial mineral reserves in Japan.
subfiles.summary: The airgram reproduces a news item released on December 3, 1949, by the Public Information Office of General Headquarters, U.S. Far East Command, under the punning headline “The Page to Help Geologists.” It announces that Ben M. Page, Director of Stanford University’s Geological Survey, had arrived in Japan to assist the Mining and Geology Division of the Natural Resources Section. His assignment covered improved exploration for copper, lead, zinc, iron, manganese, graphite, and nonmetallic minerals, as well as coordination of recommendations made by earlier American experts. He was to work closely with the Japanese Geological Survey and the Metals and Industrial Minerals Exploration Advisory Committee.

interest: The document provides a compact example of how American occupation authorities connected scientific expertise to Japan’s postwar economic reconstruction and pursuit of industrial self-sufficiency. Its unusually specific list of desired minerals makes it useful for studying occupation-era resource priorities, while its identification of cooperating Japanese agencies illustrates the institutional relationship between U.S. experts and Japan’s scientific bureaucracy. The promotional headline also shows how technical assistance was presented through occupation public-information channels.
